description: We are a team of students passionate about astronomy, physics, and technology, with skills in research, machine learning, data analysis, and visualization. For NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we aim to build an interactive website which allows users to compare infrared sky images and identify changing celestial objects. We hope to combine our strengths in research, web development, UI/UX design, and astronomical data processing to make space exploration accessible to everyone.
summary:
The universe is constantly changing, yet identifying moving celestial objects within vast astronomical datasets remains challenging. We developed SkyShift, an interactive web platform that transforms NASA's SPHEREX infrared observations into an accessible environment for scientific investigation and citizen science.

SkyShift allows users to explore real SPHEREx images, compare observations across time, visualize Gaia DR3 reference stars, and investigate celestial motion. Its integrated BlinkIR feature provides interactive image blinking, difference visualizations, guided investigations, and simulated infrared spectral exploration.

To demonstrate SkyShift's scientific capabilities, we recovered the seasonal displacement of the known white dwarf van Maanen 2 using genuine SPHEREx observations. Our analysis achieved a 5.8σ motion detection, supported by uncertainty estimates, reference-star validation, and reproducible scientific evidence.

By combing rigorous astronomical analysis with intuitive visualization, SkyShift addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by making changes in the infrared sky easier to observe, understand, and investigate. The platform creates opportunities for public participation in astronomy and provides a foundation for future searches for previously unidentified celestial objects.
details:
SkyShift is an interactive web observatory developed for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge, addressing the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It brings infrared sky observations, astronomical reference data, educational simulations, and reproducible investigation tools into one browser-based platform. Our goal is to help students, educators, and citizen scientists explore how the sky changes while understanding the evidence behind what they see.

SkyShift’s Observatory displays real SPHEREx images obtained through NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive. Users can browse observation dates, blink between compatible images, and inspect wavelength information, quality flags, and data provenance. Gaia Data Release 3 supplies reference-star positions, proper motions, and parallaxes. SkyShift propagates catalog positions to the observation dates and compares them with positions measured in the images to evaluate alignment. Our initial real-data demonstration includes 17 selected SPHEREx DR1 frames around Barnard’s Star.

The platform connects observation with explanation. Motion lab provides interactive lessons on orbital motion, proper motion, and parallax, helping users understand why an object may appear to move. The BlinkIR simulation experience adds guided examples of image blinking, difference visualizations, and illustrative infrared spectra. These demonstrations help users explore the relationships between apparent motion, brightness changes, and spectral features. The Evidence notebook preserves training measurements, assumptions, and notes through reproducible exports, while Methods presents provenance, validation results, and scientific limitations.

We developed SkyShift using Python and FastAPI for the backend, with astronomy and numerical tools including Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, and PyVO. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS, with JavaScript canvas rendering and Plotly supporting the BlinkIR experience. We used Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub for development and collaboration, and pytest, Vitest, and Playwright for automated verification. Claude Code and ChatGPT assisted with implementation, planning, and documentation. Development used standard personal computers; visitors access the platform through a web browser.

SkyShift’s creativity comes from connecting a scientific investigation’s stages: observing a change, exploring its possible explanation, checking the supporting information, and preserving a record. Users can move between real observations and educational demonstrations within the same environment.

Our team considered accessibility, usability, performance, reproducibility, and scientific accuracy. We paid particular attention to wavelength compatibility, observation timing, coordinate conventions, saturation, image artifacts, and measurement uncertainty. We also emphasized clear distinctions between real observations, catalog predictions, and synthetic demonstrations.

SkyShift’s intended impact is to make public astronomical data easier to explore and scientific reasoning easier to practice. It supports classroom learning and public participation in astronomy, while providing a foundation for future investigations of moving celestial sources. We acknowledge NASA/IPAC IRSA and ESA/Gaia/DPAC for the data that make this work possible.
